content: 1. Dispensing of tuberculosis (TB) preventive therapy should include documentation of the dates when therapy was initiated and completed. 2. Counseling on reproductive and family planning options should be provided to patients. 3. TB status should be assessed and recorded for all patients. 4. Counseling on infant feeding practices should be conducted, and adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be reinforced through counseling sessions. 5. Malaria prevention counseling should be provided, and syphilis testing and treatment results should be documented. 6. Intermittent preventive therapy for malaria (IPTp) should be dispensed, and insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) should be provided or referrals made for their acquisition. 7. At the time of labor and delivery (L&D) or postpartum, HIV status at admission should be recorded, along with the date of confirmed positive HIV test results or the date of HIV testing and its outcome. 8. The date of ART initiation and the specific antiretroviral (ARV) regimen should be documented. 9. Counseling on infant feeding practices and the actual feeding practices should be recorded, along with the provision of infant ARV prophylaxis, including the date and type of drug dispensed. 10. Reproductive and family planning choices should be documented, and referrals to HIV care should be made when applicable. 11. TB status and the dates of initiation and completion of TB preventive therapy should be recorded. 12. Maternal HIV status and syphilis test results, as well as maternal syphilis treatment, should be documented on child health cards. 13. The infant’s date of birth, infant feeding counseling (with dates), and infant feeding practices (with dates recorded) should be noted. 14. Maternal ART initiation date and ARV regimen should be recorded. 15. Infant ARV prophylaxis, including the date and type of drug dispensed, should be documented. 16. The infant’s age in weeks or months at the time of HIV testing, the type of HIV test performed, and the test results should be recorded. 17. The infant’s age in weeks or months when cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis was initiated should be documented. 18. The final outcome status of the infant, the date of enrollment in HIV care, and the infant’s unique ID should be recorded. 19. The infant’s ART initiation date, TB status, and the dates of initiation and completion of TB preventive therapy should be documented. 20. For HIV-exposed infants, the date of birth, registration number, mother’s unique ID, and the infant’s name should be recorded. 21. The mother’s ART initiation date and whether maternal ART was maintained at 3 and 12 months postpartum should be documented. 22. HIV-exposed infant ARV prophylaxis, including the date and type of drug dispensed, should be recorded. 23. Infant feeding practices at 3 months (DTP3 visit) and the age in weeks or months when CTX prophylaxis was initiated should be documented. 24. TB status and the dates of initiation and completion of TB preventive therapy should be recorded. 25. The infant’s HIV test results, the age in weeks or months at the time of testing, and the type of HIV test performed should be documented. 26. High comorbidity and mortality due to HIV-associated TB necessitate an integrated approach to service delivery and patient monitoring. 27. WHO recommends 12 collaborative TB/HIV activities monitored by global, national, and optional indicators, as outlined in the WHO Guide to Monitoring and Evaluation of Collaborative TB/HIV Activities. 28. Monitoring of HIV among TB patients is based on standardized TB patient treatment cards, registers, and reports using globally standardized definitions. 29. Coordination of care, treatment, and patient monitoring between TB and HIV services should be established to ensure effective management of both diseases. 30. Electronic data systems can facilitate integrated patient monitoring, capturing information on HIV prevention, diagnosis, care, and referral within TB programs, as well as TB screening, prevention, and treatment within HIV care/ART programs. 31. WHO recommends that an HIV patient card be initiated for all patients testing HIV-positive at TB clinics, and once ART is started, they should be entered into an ART register. 32. Early warning indicators (EWIs) of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) should be monitored annually at all ART clinics or a representative sample of clinics in a country. 33. Surveillance for pretreatment HIVDR in adults initiating first-line ART, acquired HIVDR in adults and children on treatment, and HIVDR in infants under 18 months should be conducted. 34. Monitoring of EWIs provides a record of clinic and program performance, helping to contextualize results from national HIVDR surveillance. 35. Gaps in clinic and program-level performance should prompt appropriate investigations and public health actions to improve ART service delivery quality and minimize preventable HIVDR. 36. WHO recommends that EWIs be reported on a census of patients where resources and data quality are adequate. 37. Resources should be directed at strengthening routine patient monitoring systems rather than creating parallel systems for EWI data collection and reporting. 38. Countries should harmonize the collection and reporting of these indicators by validating, strengthening, and using routine patient monitoring systems. 39. An EWI data abstraction tool in Microsoft Excel format provided by WHO facilitates data abstraction and automatically assigns performance classifications (green, amber, red) for given indicators. 40. Countries should make every effort to harmonize the collection and reporting of these indicators by validating and strengthening routine patient monitoring systems.
